title: QueryForge
description: A complete relational database engine — lexer, Pratt parser, a statistics-driven cost-based optimizer with cost-based join reordering (Selinger-style subset DP), index-only (covering) scans, bitmap-AND of multiple indexes and composite B+Tree indexes, a Volcano-model executor with hash & sort-merge joins, an external merge sort, GROUPING SETS/ROLLUP/CUBE with GROUPING(), ordered-set aggregates (PERCENTILE_CONT/DISC, MODE), correlated subqueries, CTEs (incl. WITH RECURSIVE), set operations, standard-grade window functions, statistical aggregates with FILTER, transactions, CSV import, an SVG chart view and an EXPLAIN visualizer. First-class temporal types — DATE, TIME, TIMESTAMP and INTERVAL as tagged values that index, sort, group and join like any column — with typed literals, calendar-aware date arithmetic (month-clamping), EXTRACT/DATE_TRUNC/AGE, MAKE_* constructors and CURRENT_DATE/TIMESTAMP. Full declarative integrity: PRIMARY KEY/UNIQUE (composite), CHECK and DEFAULT, and FOREIGN KEYs with ON DELETE/UPDATE referential actions (CASCADE/RESTRICT/SET NULL/SET DEFAULT, recursively), ALTER TABLE schema evolution, and atomic statements that roll back wholesale on any constraint failure. And first-class exact numerics: arbitrary-precision DECIMAL/NUMERIC (BigInt-backed) where 0.1 + 0.2 is exactly 0.3 and money SUMs never lose a cent — DECIMAL(p,s) columns, exact arithmetic & aggregates, and Postgres-style TO_CHAR currency formatting. Plus VIEWs (CREATE [OR REPLACE] VIEW, inlined wherever they're used, even inside other views), UPSERT (INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING / DO UPDATE with EXCLUDED), and an optimizer that decorrelates a correlated [NOT] EXISTS into a single hash SemiJoin / AntiJoin instead of re-running the subquery per row. And now first-class JSON (jsonb-style): a tagged, normalized value (sorted/de-duplicated keys) that indexes, sorts, groups, joins and persists like any column, with the path/containment operators (-> ->> #> #>> @> <@ ?), a Postgres ::TYPE postfix cast, a scalar/aggregate library (JSON_BUILD_OBJECT/ARRAY, JSON_EXTRACT_PATH, JSONB_SET, JSON_PRETTY, JSON_AGG, JSON_OBJECT_AGG, …) and set-returning table functions in FROM (JSON_ARRAY_ELEMENTS, JSON_EACH, …) that unnest JSON into rows. And now first-class FULL-TEXT SEARCH (Postgres tsvector/tsquery): two more tagged values threaded through the same value plumbing so a search document indexes, sorts, groups, joins and persists like any column — built on a from-scratch Porter (1980) stemmer, an English stop-word list and a positional tokenizer. The @@ match operator does boolean (& | !), prefix (:*), weight-filtered (:A) and true positional PHRASE search (a <-> b, a <N> b) via a position-set executor; to_tsvector / to_tsquery / plainto_tsquery / phraseto_tsquery / websearch_to_tsquery build documents and queries; ts_rank / ts_rank_cd rank by A/B/C/D weights and cover density; ts_headline highlights; setweight / strip / || shape vectors. The capstone is a real GIN inverted index (CREATE INDEX … USING GIN) — maintained on every insert/update/delete and across snapshots — that the planner turns into a posting-list candidate probe plus an exact recheck (a GinScan in EXPLAIN), so search is sublinear yet byte-for-byte identical to the sequential-scan filter. And now STANDARD-GRADE WINDOW FUNCTIONS: a from-scratch frame engine with all three modes — ROWS (physical), RANGE (typed value offsets over numbers, exact DECIMAL and DATE/TIMESTAMP ± INTERVAL, honouring ASC/DESC) and GROUPS (peer groups) — each with the EXCLUDE clause (NO OTHERS / CURRENT ROW / GROUP / TIES), aggregate FILTER (WHERE …) in the frame, IGNORE NULLS / RESPECT NULLS value functions (FIRST_VALUE/LAST_VALUE/NTH_VALUE/LAG/LEAD), the statistical (STDDEV/VARIANCE) and ordered-set (PERCENTILE_CONT/DISC, MODE) families as windows, and a named WINDOW clause with reference inheritance (OVER (w …)) — all proven against the GROUP BY aggregates in self-tests. And now first-class ARRAY types (T[]): a fifth tagged value — nestable, so multi-dimensional — threaded through the same value plumbing so an array column indexes, sorts, groups, joins and persists like any other, with a Postgres element-wise total order. The ARRAY[…] constructor and {…} text literals build them; 1-based subscripts a[i] and inclusive slices a[lo:hi] read them; the containment/overlap operators (@> <@ &&) and the array-operand quantifiers (x = ANY(a), x < ALL(a)) test them with full three-valued logic; || concatenates (array‖array, array‖elem, elem‖array). A full function library — array_length / cardinality / array_ndims / array_dims, array_append / prepend / cat / remove / replace, array_position(s) / trim_array, array_to_string / string_to_array — plus the array_agg aggregate (ordered, NULL-keeping, DISTINCT) and the set-returning unnest() / generate_subscripts() table functions (so LATERAL unnest(t.col) expands a column into rows), with to_json / ::json interop. The capstone is a GIN inverted index over an array column (CREATE INDEX … USING GIN) — maintained on every insert/update/delete and across snapshots — that the planner turns into a posting-list candidate probe (AND for @>, OR for && / = ANY) plus an exact recheck (a GinScan in EXPLAIN), so array search is sublinear yet byte-for-byte identical to the sequential-scan filter. And now a from-scratch MVCC CONCURRENCY ENGINE with an interactive Concurrency Lab: per-key version chains (xmin/xmax) with snapshot visibility, the four isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED → SERIALIZABLE) including Serializable Snapshot Isolation (Cahill's rw-antidependency graph with the PostgreSQL dangerous-structure pivot rule), first-updater-wins write conflicts, lock-wait blocking with waits-for deadlock detection, and a deterministic schedule runner that drives canonical anomaly scenarios (dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update, write skew, deadlock, the read-only anomaly) — visualized as a transaction timeline, a live version-chain inspector, an rw-conflict graph and a serializability verdict, so you watch each anomaly appear and vanish as you raise the isolation level. And now a LEVELLED-UP COST-BASED OPTIMIZER with an interactive Optimizer Lab: a System-R distinct-value join-cardinality model (|L|·|R| / max(V(L),V(R)), with each key's distinct count capped by its input's surviving rows, so a selective filter finally propagates through a join), an INDEX NESTED-LOOP JOIN (a tiny outer driver probes a large inner table's B+Tree on the join key — one index descent per outer row instead of hashing the whole inner side, chosen by cost), and a what-if INDEX ADVISOR (HypoPG / SQL-Server-DTA style) that enumerates candidate indexes from a query's equalities, ranges, join keys and ORDER BY, builds each one hypothetically (a real backfilled B+Tree, retracted the instant the plan is costed — your data is never touched), re-plans, and recommends only the indexes the optimizer would actually adopt at a lower cost, each with a ready-to-run CREATE INDEX and one-click Apply. The Optimizer Lab makes it legible — the chosen plan with per-operator cost, a replay of the join-order subset-DP search (every relation subset, its cheapest sub-plan, the order it settled on), and the advisor's ranked recommendations (including an index that flips a hash join into a cheaper index nested-loop join). And now a from-scratch ARIES WRITE-AHEAD LOGGING & CRASH-RECOVERY engine with an interactive Recovery Lab: single-cell pages with pageLSNs, a forced on-disk log vs. a volatile tail, a STEAL/NO-FORCE buffer pool (so a crash needs both REDO and UNDO), the write-ahead rule on page flush, log-forcing commits and fuzzy checkpoints — recovered by the canonical three passes (Analysis rebuilds the dirty-page/transaction tables and the RedoLSN; Redo repeats history, winners and losers alike, idempotently via the pageLSN test; Undo rolls losers back in reverse-LSN order logging redo-only CLRs with undoNextLSN, so a crash *during* recovery resumes without double-undoing). The Recovery Lab scrubs a workload → crash → recovery as one timeline — a phase rail, a live log (durable/volatile/recovery-written), disk+buffer page images, the rebuilt tables, and a verdict that checks the recovered state against an independently computed correct outcome. And now MEMORY-BOUNDED EXECUTION with an interactive Execution Lab: a SET work_mem row-budget knob that makes every blocking operator spill to "disk" instead of materializing an unbounded working set — a top-N heapsort (ORDER BY … LIMIT keeps only the top k rows in a bounded heap, provably identical to a full sort then slice), a work_mem-bounded external merge sort, a grace HASH AGGREGATE (overflow group keys are hash-partitioned and spilled, then each partition re-aggregated — so a huge GROUP BY stays exact, COUNT(DISTINCT) and all), and a grace HASH JOIN (both inputs partitioned by the join-key hash and joined partition-by-partition, NULL keys streamed separately so every outer-join flavour is preserved), all recursing on skew. EXPLAIN ANALYZE carries per-operator memory accounting (peak rows, spilled rows, partitions, passes); the Execution Lab drags a work_mem slider and shows the plan switch from in-memory to spilling with live memory bars, while a side-by-side unbounded run proves the answer is identical multiset for multiset. Plus a safe statement (parse) cache for repeated read-only queries. And now a SECOND, INDEPENDENT EXECUTION ENGINE — a from-scratch VECTORIZED (columnar) executor with an interactive Vectorize Lab: the whole database runs the Volcano (row-at-a-time iterator) model, the textbook slow path for analytics, so the analytic subset (single table; numeric WHERE / GROUP BY / aggregates) also runs the MonetDB/X100 → DuckDB way — a relation transposed once into packed Float64Array columns, batches of a column pushed through type-specialized kernels compiled as closures over the captured typed arrays (col[i] directly — no boxed SqlValue, no generic comparator), a filter narrowing an Int32Array selection vector instead of copying rows, and a GROUP BY keyed on the numeric tuple by a native open-addressing hash table (no per-row string key) accumulating COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX into flat typed arrays, order-preservingly so even a floating-point SUM matches the row engine bit-for-bit. A conservative analyzer runs only what it can prove it matches and falls back to Volcano otherwise; a differential self-test group runs queries through both engines asserting identical multisets; and the Vectorize Lab races them live over a large dataset — an identical-result verdict, Volcano-vs-vectorized timing and throughput bars, the speedup factor (20×+ on group-by roll-ups), and a vector-width sweep chart showing the cache-residency sweet spot. And now the database TESTS ITSELF — a from-scratch METAMORPHIC SQL FUZZER with an interactive Fuzz Lab: it builds a random database from a 32-bit seed (deterministic, replayable byte-for-byte) and throws thousands of random queries at the engine, each checked against an oracle that needs no reference answer — TLP (ternary-logic partitioning: a scan equals the multiset-union of its p / NOT p / p IS NULL partitions, and aggregates are partition-additive), NoREC (a WHERE count must equal the same predicate demoted to a CASE-sum the optimizer can't touch), DISTINCT-vs-dedup, and OPT-DIFF (the same query under SET optimizer = on vs off must agree). This is SQLancer's technique (Rigger & Su, 2020, 450+ real bugs in SQLite/Postgres/MySQL/DuckDB) — and on its first run it found three real NULL/index-range bugs in QueryForge, all now fixed and frozen as regression tests, with any new counterexample automatically delta-debugged to a minimal repro. Plus generate_series(start, stop[, step]) — the workhorse set-returning function for integers and calendar-aware timestamp ranges. And now a THIRD, INDEPENDENT EXECUTION ENGINE — a from-scratch QUERY COMPILER (JIT) with an interactive Compile Lab: where the database interprets a plan (row-at-a-time Volcano, or column-batch vectorized), this path takes the data-centric "compiling query plans into machine code" road (Neumann, VLDB 2011 — the model behind HyPer / Spark whole-stage codegen / Postgres JIT), walking a matched SELECT once and emitting a JavaScript function that fuses the WHOLE pipeline into one loop — dimension hash tables built inline, INNER equi-joins probed inside the driving scan (nested for left-deep multi-joins), the WHERE re-checked on the assembled row, and COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX folded into a group's inlined accumulator fields — then new Function()s it so the browser's own JIT lowers it to machine code, with the generated source shown on screen. It is conservative by construction (an analyzer returns a reason and the caller falls back to Volcano for anything outside its subset) and correct by construction (expression leaves reuse the canonical evaluator so three-valued logic and every tagged type match the interpreter byte-for-byte; NULL join keys never match; SUM/AVG gated to INTEGER/REAL so float accumulation is identical, DECIMAL falling back to the exact path). A 33-case differential self-test group runs every supported shape through both engines asserting identical multisets (plus negative cases proving the unsupported shapes fall back), and the Compile Lab races them live on a star-schema join, a two-dimension snowflake and a hash-aggregate roll-up — an identical-result verdict, Volcano-vs-compiled timing bars, the fused-pipeline steps, and the speedup (≈6–7× on the star join, ≈5× on the snowflake, ≈14× on the hash-aggregate roll-up) with codegen itself under a millisecond. And now a SELF-BALANCING B+TREE with an interactive Storage Lab: the index B+Tree every access path rides used to delete LAZILY (pull the entry, never rebalance), so a churned index drifted toward half-empty nodes and only got shallower by luck; now a delete that drops a node below ⌈order/2⌉ slots BORROWS a key from a fuller sibling (fixing the parent separator) or MERGES with one and pulls the separator down, COLLAPSING the root when it is left with a single child — so an emptied tree returns to height 1 and every non-root node stays at least half full. A bottom-up bulkLoad packs a sorted run into leaves at a target fill factor (how a real CREATE INDEX builds), a checkInvariants() structural oracle proves balance / key order / separator routing / equal leaf depth / a sorted leaf chain, and insert/delete record a replayable structural trace. The Storage Lab draws the LIVE tree as an SVG — internal separators, leaf cells, the dashed leaf chain — and lets you insert, delete, bulk-load and range-scan it (the scan lights up the leaf chain it walks) while a guided demo steps through growth → borrow → merge → collapse, each step narrated from the tree's own trace and re-proven by an after-every-step ✓ valid B+Tree badge. The new `storage` self-test group holds it to the suite's highest bar: a differential oracle (the tree must answer search/range exactly like a brute-force sorted array) AND the invariant checker run after EVERY mutation across thousands of seeded random insert/delete operations at several fanouts. And now INCREMENTAL MATERIALIZED VIEWS with an interactive IVM Lab: where a plain VIEW is inlined (recomputed wherever it is used), a CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW stores its result and keeps it correct by computing the DELTA to the view from the DELTA to the base — never a recompute — the data-centric DBSP / Z-set model (Budiu et al., VLDB 2023). A from-scratch Z-set algebra (a bag with integer weights, negative = retraction) turns σ/π/⋈ into linear maps; a single MatViewManager poked by the catalog's three row-level mutators maintains every view through every write path (DML, UPSERT, MERGE, and FK cascade chains, which telescope to the exact answer); σ and π push a delta straight through, the join reads the other relations live (single-occurrence ⇒ linear) with predicate push-down, and aggregation keeps O(groups) running state — exact integer SUM/AVG, plus MIN/MAX value-multisets so a deleted extreme recovers the next one — emitting a retract+insert only for the groups a delta touches. SELECT … FROM mv scans the stored, maintained contents as a true materialized relation; REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW is the from-scratch oracle; a transaction rollback re-derives views from their definitions so they stay exact. An eligibility analyzer vets each query for the maintainable SPJ-A subset and rejects anything else with a precise reason. The new `ivm` differential self-test group proves a maintained view equals a recompute byte-for-byte across targeted edge cases (group-key moves, min/max retraction, FK cascade, rollback, snapshot round-trip) and a six-seed fuzz (five view shapes re-checked after every one of 40 random mutations); the IVM Lab lets you mutate base rows and watch each view update by just the changed rows with a live identical-multiset verdict. And now the IVM engine goes well beyond the integer SPJ-A core: a single LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER JOIN is maintained by tracking each preserved-side row's live match count (so its NULL-extended image flips as its last/first match arrives or leaves), SUM/AVG are exact over DECIMAL as well as INTEGER (a BigInt-backed running total that never drifts under retraction), and a grouped view now maintains COUNT(DISTINCT), an aggregate FILTER (WHERE …), a HAVING threshold (a group flips in/out as it crosses) and arbitrary scalar projections over its keys and aggregates — each held to the same byte-for-byte differential bar (the fuzz now re-checks 13 view shapes after every one of 50 random mutations on two tables), with a MaterializedView.explain() rendering the compiled incremental dataflow as an EXPLAIN-style tree in the Lab. And now the IVM engine maintains SELF-JOINS and runs a SUBLINEAR, DELTA-DRIVEN DATAFLOW: a table joined to itself is kept correct by the bilinear cross-term — when a base table T occupying k slots changes by ΔT, the view delta is the binomial expansion over the nonempty subsets of those slots (ΔT⋈T_old + T_old⋈ΔT + ΔT⋈ΔT for a self-join, generalized to any multiplicity), read off a per-view integrated mirror that holds the pre-delta state — and every equijoin becomes a graph edge with a hash index on its join key, maintained in lock-step, so a base delta drives the join from the (tiny) changed side and PROBES the others by index (O(matches), not O(other table)) instead of nested-looping them. The probe only narrows candidates (every predicate is still rechecked, NULL keys excluded), so it is a pure speed-up the differential fuzz proves identical — measured flat-cost maintenance as the joined table grows 64×, surfaced as a Δ-probe annotation in EXPLAIN and an order_pairs self-join showcase in the IVM Lab. And now APPROXIMATE QUERY PROCESSING — a from-scratch, standalone SKETCH ENGINE of probabilistic, sublinear, mergeable data summaries with an interactive Sketch Lab: HyperLogLog (COUNT DISTINCT in 2^p one-byte registers, error ≈1.04/√m, register-max merge), Count–Min (one-sided point frequency in a d×w grid, min over rows, conservative update, ≤ ε·N over-estimate), Space-Saving (top-k heavy hitters in O(k) slots, every true frequency > N/k guaranteed found), a t-digest (tail-accurate p99/p999 quantiles via asin-scaled variable-width centroids), reservoir sampling (Algorithm R + weighted A-Res) and a Bloom filter (membership with zero false negatives + a Bloom semijoin) — all riding a strong from-scratch 64-bit MurmurHash over the engine's canonical value encoding, every one a monoid so partial summaries merge. The headline sketches are wired into SQL as APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT (HLL), APPROX_PERCENTILE WITHIN GROUP (t-digest), APPROX_TOP_K(x, k) (Space-Saving, returning a JSON array of {value, count}) and a TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI/SYSTEM/RESERVOIR [REPEATABLE(seed)] clause (a Sample operator that samples the physical table before WHERE, so the vectorized/compiled engines and IVM decline it), each cross-checked against the exact aggregate within its error bound; the Sketch Lab makes the memory-vs-accuracy trade watchable — pick a sketch and a distribution and see the estimate close on the truth as the footprint grows. And now WORST-CASE-OPTIMAL JOINS — a from-scratch, standalone WCOJ ENGINE with an interactive WCOJ Lab: every join elsewhere is binary (a tree of two-way operators), which Atserias–Grohe–Marx / Ngo–Porat–Ré–Rudra proved sub-optimal on cyclic queries — the smallest binary plan still builds an intermediate bigger than the final answer (the triangle: output ≤ N^{3/2}, but any two-way join first materializes up to N²). QueryForge builds the whole theory from scratch: a sorted-array trie with the paper's O(log n) linear iterator, a Leapfrog unary join (round-robin k-way sorted intersection), the Leapfrog Triejoin (Veldhuizen / LogicBlox — variable-at-a-time elimination that runs in O(AGM bound) and never builds an intermediate bigger than its answer), and the AGM bound itself via a from-scratch two-phase simplex solving the fractional-edge-cover LP (ρ* = 3/2 for the triangle, 3 for a star, 2 for a k-cycle). It runs over the engine's own total value order, so joins work over every SQL type; the wcoj self-test group proves the triejoin equal to a binary-join reference AND to the SQL executor's own DISTINCT join across thousands of seeded instances (triangle/4-cycle/path/star/4-clique), the simplex against closed-form optima, and the AGM bound theorem (output ≤ bound); the WCOJ Lab renders the query hypergraph, the fractional cover, the variable-elimination trace, and — on the adversarial dense grid — the binary intermediate blow-up (576 rows for a 24-row triangle answer) a worst-case-optimal join provably dodges. And now a SECOND STORAGE ENGINE — a from-scratch LOG-STRUCTURED MERGE (LSM) TREE with an interactive LSM Lab: the B+Tree is read-optimized and updates in place, so QueryForge builds its mirror image, the write-optimized structure behind LevelDB/RocksDB/Cassandra/ScyllaDB. An LSM never updates in place — a write appends to an in-memory skip-list memtable; a full memtable flushes sequentially to an immutable sorted SSTable at level 0; and background compaction merges SSTables down a level hierarchy, reconciling overwrites and deletions. A monotonic sequence number gives a total newest-wins order across every level, and a tombstone carries a delete down until it reaches a level with nothing beneath it (LevelDB's IsBaseLevelForKey, generalized to a key range) where it is reclaimed; a major compaction (RocksDB CompactRange) merges everything into one run, leaving exactly one entry per live key. The read cost — a key may live in several tables at once — is clawed back per SSTable by fence pointers (min/max key skip a table whose range can't hold the key), a Bloom filter sized to a target FPR with a proven zero-false-negatives guarantee (a probable miss becomes an O(1) 'no'), and a sparse per-block index (a hit is a binary search plus one block scan); range reads and compaction share one k-way merging iterator that reconciles the memtable and every SSTable to the newest live version. Three compaction strategies ship — leveled (non-overlapping runs, low read/space amp), size-tiered (overlapping runs merged wholesale, low write amp) and lazy-leveled (Dostoevsky — tiered shallow, one leveled run at the largest level, near-tiered writes with near-leveled reads/space) — behind a toggle, plus a RUM-trade-off benchmark that races all three on one deterministic workload and proves they return byte-identical live state while measuring write/read/space amplification. The lsm self-test group holds it to the storage bar: a differential oracle (point + range reads must match a last-write-wins reference) AND a structural invariant checker run after every mutation across thousands of seeded random ops under both strategies, plus the Bloom guarantee, the SSTable block-index/fences, the merge's newest-wins reconciliation and exact major compaction; the LSM Lab draws the memtable as skip-list express lanes, each level's SSTables as cards (key range, entry count, Bloom fill, tombstone marker), lights up a point lookup's read path (which tables it read vs. skipped by Bloom/fence), and tracks live write/read/space amplification. And now the WHOLE FAMILY OF CONCURRENCY-CONTROL PROTOCOLS with an interactive Protocols Lab: the MVCC engine was only one protocol, so QueryForge builds the rest from scratch as a standalone module against the same interleaved-schedule model, running one schedule through four protocols at once — Strict 2PL (a from-scratch shared/exclusive lock manager with S→X upgrades, locks held to commit, a coarse predicate lock on a synthetic index guard for phantoms, and waits-for-graph deadlock detection), OCC (Kung–Robinson read/validate/write phases with backward validation, lock-free and cascadeless), Basic Timestamp Ordering (per-item read/write timestamps + the Thomas write rule — the deliberate outlier that permits dirty reads and so must cascade-abort, serializable yet not recoverable), and the existing MVCC/SSI adapted as a fourth column at any isolation level. The load-bearing piece is a protocol-independent conflict-serializability oracle — a precedence-graph acyclicity check that certifies every protocol's committed history is serializable and topologically sorts an equivalent serial order; a generic deterministic scheduler drives all lock-based engines, and a seeded random-schedule generator fuzzes them. The Protocols Lab is a four-column head-to-head — each column's verdict + equivalent serial order, live metrics (commits/aborts/blocks/deadlocks/validation-fails), per-transaction outcomes, a colour-coded trace, the final committed state and its correctness-guarantee badges — with an MVCC isolation-level selector (watch snapshot isolation admit write skew below SERIALIZABLE) and a 🎲 random-schedule fuzzer; the protocols self-test group fuzzes 600+ random schedules proving every protocol serializable, the strict protocols equal to a serial replay, and 2PL/OCC never cascading while T/O sometimes must (and mid-build the fuzzer caught a real lock-manager dirty-read bug, now fixed). And now a COLUMN STORE with an interactive Columnar Lab: the physical storage layout behind every analytical engine (Parquet, ORC, DuckDB, ClickHouse, Vertica), built from scratch as a standalone module. A table is sliced into row groups; inside each group every column is encoded INDEPENDENTLY by a Parquet/ORC-family codec — PLAIN, DICTIONARY (distinct values + bit-packed codes), RLE (run-length), BITPACK/frame-of-reference (subtract the group min, pack the residuals in ⌈log₂(max−min)⌉ bits) and DELTA (a first value + bit-packed ZigZag deltas) — all riding a genuine, byte-level bit-packer that writes tight LSB-first bitstreams, so decode is a true round-trip; an auto-encoder builds every legal candidate and keeps the smallest, exactly as a real column-store writer picks a codec per chunk, and a monotone key collapses to DELTA while a low-cardinality category collapses to DICTIONARY/RLE and a wide integer to frame-of-reference. Each group carries a min/max ZONE MAP, so a scan does three things a row store can't: column projection (only the touched columns are decoded), zone-map pruning (a group whose range can't satisfy the predicate is skipped whole, never decoded — Parquet's row-group stats / ORC's row index / the data skipping of every analytical engine), and late materialization (evaluate the predicate on the predicate columns first, then fetch the projected columns only at the surviving row offsets via a random-access decode). Every one only ever changes the COST — the columnar self-test group proves a full predicate scan equals a brute-force filter over the original rows across thousands of seeded predicate conjunctions and projections, that a pruned group provably holds ZERO matches (so pruning can never change an answer), that every codec round-trips byte-for-byte over columns of every SQL value type (integers, reals, text, DECIMAL, DATE, JSON) with NULLs, and that the auto-encoder always picks the true minimum; the Columnar Lab makes it legible — the auto-encoder's per-column codec choice with a size-vs-encoding bar for each, the aggregate compression ratio vs a row store, and a live predicate that lights up each row group as scanned or pruned with the data-skipping percentage and the fraction of cells actually decoded. Proven by 622 in-app self-tests (including the protocols group; the lsm group — differential + structural invariants after every mutation under all three compaction strategies, the zero-false-negatives Bloom guarantee, seq-shadowing, exact major compaction, and a benchmark proving the three strategies agree on live state while their amplification profiles match the RUM trade-off — the wcoj group, the sketch group's per-sketch bounds vs an exact oracle, the IVM fuzz across sixteen view shapes, and seven B+Tree/SQL fuzz sweeps re-checking ~1,750 random queries every build). Built from scratch in TypeScript, running entirely in the browser.
